name: Government Open Data Licence - India (GODL-India)
publisher: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology / NIC, Open Government Data Platform India
caveats: Canonical page www.data.gov.in/Godl was EGRESS_BLOCKED this session; licence text below is from a Wikipedia template mirror plus search extracts
Licence covers 'shareable non-sensitive data' only - the exemptions clause carves out personal data and third-party IP, so GODL is NOT authority for processing FIR-level personal data
Exact exemptions clause, no-endorsement clause and governing-law clause are UNVERIFIED and must be read from the gazette text
No share-alike obligation, so our derived layers need not be open
evidence: Wikipedia Template:GODL-India confirms grant wording 'worldwide, royalty-free, non-exclusive license to use, adapt, publish ... for all lawful commercial and non-commercial purposes', attribution obligation requiring DOI/URL/URI, and that providers 'are not liable for any errors or omissions'. Search extracts from jk.data.gov.in/godl and smartcities.data.gov.in give gazette notification 13 February 2017 and confirm derivative works including 'products and services' are permitted.
how_to_obtain: A human in India (or any network without the .gov.in egress block) opens https://www.data.gov.in/Godl and saves the full clause-numbered text plus the gazette notification PDF to research/_raw/. Mirrors at jk.data.gov.in/godl and smartcities.data.gov.in/government-open-data-license-india carry the same text.
notes: Commercial use and derivative works are expressly permitted. The single binding obligation is per-dataset attribution with a resolvable identifier - build it into the ingestion record so it renders automatically. Do not cite GODL as cover for personal data.

name: National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy (NDSAP) 2012
publisher: Department of Science & Technology, Government of India
caveats: It is a POLICY, not a statute - not directly judicially enforceable on its own
Negative list expressly excludes personal information, sensitive data, official symbols, IP-encumbered data, military insignia, identity documents, and anything that would violate RTI Act s.8
Its operative teeth come from the gazette-notified GODL and from RTI Act s.4(2) proactive disclosure, not from NDSAP itself
evidence: Fetched en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Data_Sharing_and_Accessibility_Policy. Confirms Cabinet approval 9 February 2012, notification 17 March 2012, scope 'all shareable non-sensitive data ... generated using public funds', the seven-item negative list, and that NDSAP is policy while the accompanying GODL (Feb 2017) was a formal Gazette notification.
how_to_obtain: Freely downloadable; the canonical PDF sits on dst.gov.in and data.gov.in, both EGRESS_BLOCKED this session.
notes: Best used in an RTI first appeal, combined with RTI s.4(2), to argue a department should already have published a dataset in machine-readable form. See rti-playbook.

name: Copyright Act 1957 - ss.2(k), 17(d), 28, 52(1)(q) (government works and the reproduction exception)
publisher: Parliament of India / Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
caveats: indiankanoon.org and copyright.gov.in both EGRESS_BLOCKED this session; only s.52(1)(q)(iv) and s.2(k) confirmed via search extract
India has NO US-style 'edicts of government' public-domain rule - a government report IS copyrighted (s.17(d)), for 60 years from first publication (s.28, UNVERIFIED)

Whether an NCRB annual statistical volume falls within s.52(1)(q)(iii) 'report of any committee, commission, council, board or other like body appointed by the Government' is the open question that decides whether we can reproduce it wholesale
evidence: Search extract from indiankanoon.org/doc/648494 confirms s.52(1)(q) permits reproduction or publication of any judgment or order of a court, Tribunal or other judicial authority unless prohibited by that body, and that s.2(k) defines a Government work as one made or published under the direction or control of any Court, tribunal or other judicial authority in India.
how_to_obtain: Read the consolidated bare Act on indiacode.nic.in or copyright.gov.in from an unblocked network; confirm the full text of s.52(1)(q) limbs (i)-(iv) and ss.17(d), 28.
notes: Facts are not copyrightable. The numbers in an NCRB volume are free. Extract the facts, rebuild our own schema and presentation, cite volume/year/table, and do not host bulk mirrors of the original PDFs.

name: IT Act 2000 ss.43(b) and 66 - unauthorised downloading/extraction of data (the India scraping exposure)
publisher: Parliament of India / MeitY
caveats: Section text UNVERIFIED - primary sources EGRESS_BLOCKED
There is no CFAA equivalent and no hiQ v LinkedIn in India; the authorisation question is undecided
s.43(b) has no damage threshold and no dishonesty requirement - it is civil compensation for downloading/copying/extracting data 'without permission of the owner'
s.66 makes the same acts criminal (up to 3 years) when done dishonestly or fraudulently
OPEN QUESTION: does a browsewrap ToU prohibiting automated access negate 'permission of the owner' for s.43(b)? No Indian authority either way.
evidence: Wikipedia's IT Act article was fetched but does not quote ss.43 or 66. Section content recorded from the agent's corpus and flagged.
how_to_obtain: Read ss.43, 43A, 66 on indiacode.nic.in from an unblocked network; ask counsel for any Indian authority on ToU and 'permission of the owner'.
notes: Mitigation is behavioural and evidentiary: obey robots.txt, identifiable User-Agent with contact URL, hard rate limit, never defeat a CAPTCHA, and write to each state SCRB/CID requesting the data or written permission. An unanswered documented request in the file materially changes how a court reads 'dishonestly'.

name: Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (Act 22 of 2023)
publisher: Parliament of India / MeitY
caveats: Primary text EGRESS_BLOCKED; section numbering below is UNVERIFIED and from the agent's corpus

s.3(c)(ii) is the central provision: the Act does not apply to personal data made publicly available by (A) the Data Principal, or (B) any person under an obligation under any law in force in India to make it publicly available
Whether a downstream re-publisher inherits that exemption is UNDECIDED - no Board decision, no judgment
THE ACT CONTAINS NO JOURNALISM EXEMPTION (unlike GDPR Art.85 and unlike the 2018 Srikrishna draft). A public-interest crime map cannot shelter behind a media carve-out
THE ACT HAS NO SENSITIVE-PERSONAL-DATA CATEGORY - caste, religion and health are ordinary personal data. No Art.22-GDPR profiling right either
s.44(3) amended RTI Act s.8(1)(j) to delete the larger-public-interest override, narrowing what RTI can extract about named individuals

s.17(2)(b) research/archiving/statistical exemption is the likeliest clean basis for an aggregate map, but only 'in accordance with such standards as may be prescribed' - those rules commence 14 May 2027
Penalties under s.33 + Schedule reportedly reach Rs 250 crore for failure to take reasonable security safeguards
evidence: Fetched en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Personal_Data_Protection_Act,_2023 - the article gives only a general overview and explicitly does not cover s.3(c)(ii), s.8, s.17 or s.33. Section detail recorded from the agent's corpus and flagged for counsel.
how_to_obtain: Read the Act on indiacode.nic.in or the e-Gazette from an unblocked network. Commission a written counsel opinion on the s.3(c)(ii) downstream question.
notes: Design rule that makes most of this moot: personal identifiers never reach durable storage. Parse in memory, persist only {category, coarse_geocode, date, source_ref, disposal_status}.

publisher: Delhi High Court, Madras High Court, Karnataka High Court, Supreme Court of India

Madras HC order 27 Feb 2024 re Indian Kanoon - STAYED by the Supreme Court 24 July 2024

name: BNS 2023 ss.72-73 (ex-IPC s.228A) - disclosure of identity of victims of sexual offences
publisher: Parliament of India / Ministry of Home Affairs
caveats: BNS s.72 prohibits printing or publishing the name OR ANY MATTER WHICH MAY MAKE KNOWN THE IDENTITY of a victim of an offence under BNS ss.64-71. Up to 2 years imprisonment AND fine

Exceptions in s.72(2): written order of the IO/officer-in-charge in good faith for investigation; the victim's written authorisation; or next of kin's written authorisation where the victim is dead, a minor or of unsound mind
s.73 (ex-IPC 228A(3)) - UNVERIFIED - prohibits publishing matter relating to court proceedings in such cases without prior court permission

Nipun Saxena v Union of India, (2019) 2 SCC 703 - UNVERIFIED - reportedly holds identity must not be disclosed even with next-of-kin consent except through the court, and extends the protection to POCSO victims
AN ADDRESS OR A SMALL AREA IS AN IDENTIFYING MATTER. In a village or a 400-household ward, category + month + location identifies the victim
evidence: Search extracts (testbook, vakilsearch, prashantkanha, legallyin) agree BNS s.72 reproduces IPC s.228A, carries up to 2 years plus fine, and has the three s.72(2) exceptions. Wikipedia's Section 228A article quotes the IPC operative words and confirms BNS s.72(1) as the successor provision. Wikipedia's Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita article confirms BNS commencement 1 July 2024.
how_to_obtain: Read BNS ss.72-73 on indiacode.nic.in; the UP Police BNS-IPC comparative PDF is the quickest mapping table but was EGRESS_BLOCKED here.
notes: THIS IS THE PROVISION THAT SETS THE MAP'S MINIMUM AGGREGATION UNIT. Sexual offences render at district level only, date aggregated to quarter, and no point geometry for any category anywhere.

name: BNS 2023 s.356 (ex-IPC ss.499-500) - defamation, and Exception 1 (truth AND public good)
publisher: Parliament of India / Ministry of Home Affairs
caveats: VERIFIED that defamation is BNS Chapter 20 s.356 and that BNS commenced 1 July 2024

UNVERIFIED detail: s.356(2) punishment is simple imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both, OR COMMUNITY SERVICE (community service is a BNS innovation); s.356(3) printing/engraving defamatory matter; s.356(4) sale of such matter

THE INDIA-SPECIFIC HAZARD: Exception 1 requires that the imputation be TRUE **and** that publication be FOR THE PUBLIC GOOD - 'whether or not it is for the public good is a question of fact'. Truth alone is NOT a complete defence to criminal defamation
Civil defamation does allow justification (truth) as a complete defence, but India has NO statutory partial-justification provision, so India is stricter than England even on the civil side

Explanation 2 (UNVERIFIED) - it may amount to defamation to make an imputation concerning a company, an association or a collection of persons as such: this is the group-defamation hook for an RWA or a builder
Subramanian Swamy v Union of India, (2016) 7 SCC 221 - UNVERIFIED citation - upheld criminal defamation as constitutional
The realistic harm is not losing but being sued: a private complaint under BNSS s.222 in a distant magistracy, summons, and years of personal appearances by directors
evidence: Fetched en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharatiya_Nyaya_Sanhita. Confirms the BNS 'comprises 20 chapters and 358 sections', that Chapter 20 covers 'Criminal Intimidation, Insult, Annoyance, Defamation, Etc' with 'Defamation (356)' listed, and that the BNS commenced 01-July-2024. The exceptions, punishment detail and Subramanian Swamy citation are NOT in the article and are flagged UNVERIFIED.
how_to_obtain: Read BNS s.356 and its Exceptions on indiacode.nic.in; the UP Police BNS-IPC comparative table gives the mapping.
notes: Mitigation is editorial: rates with denominators and CIs, 'reported crime (FIRs)' framing, no rankings, no adjectives, a methodology page, a corrections policy, and a right of reply for local bodies.

name: Group defamation standing - RWAs, builders and municipalities (and the absence of Indian map/rating precedent)
publisher: Indian courts (no controlling authority identified)
caveats: I FOUND NO REPORTED INDIAN DECISION on a crime map, an area safety rating or a neighbourhood index harming property values. Recording that as a finding, not as an absence of risk - the exposure is UNQUANTIFIED, and a first case would be one of first impression
A locality is not a legal person and cannot sue
A Resident Welfare Association usually IS a juristic person (Societies Registration Act 1860, a state Apartment Ownership Act, or a co-operative housing society statute) and can complain
A builder/developer is a company and can sue in both civil and criminal defamation over an imputation about a named project

A municipality is a statutory corporation; whether an elected governmental body can sue for defamation is answered 'no' in England by Derbyshire County Council v Times Newspapers Ltd [1993] AC 534, which is PERSUASIVE BUT NOT BINDING in India and unsettled here
Indian courts require a group to be determinate and identifiable and require the claimant to show the imputation pointed at them
evidence: No Indian precedent located. Searches on this point could not be run - the WebSearch budget was exhausted after four queries and every Indian legal database was EGRESS_BLOCKED.
how_to_obtain: Ask counsel to run a Manupatra/SCC Online search for (a) defamation suits by RWAs or housing societies, and (b) defamation suits against review or rating platforms, 2015-2026. This is one of the two items most worth a litigator's time.
notes: Because the exposure is unquantified rather than low, the mitigation is to avoid creating a determinate identifiable group: no rankings, no named-project or named-society output, no 'worst locality' framing.

name: Indian anti-discrimination law gap - redlining, tenant screening, insurance and lending
publisher: n/a - a documented absence of regulation
caveats: NO fair-housing statute, NO Equal Credit Opportunity Act equivalent, NO general disparate-impact doctrine in Indian private law

Art.15(1) binds the State; Art.15(2) reaches private denial of access to shops, restaurants, hotels and places of public entertainment and to wells/tanks/roads - NOT tenancy or lending. Art.17 abolishes untouchability

THE DPDP ACT HAS NO SENSITIVE-PERSONAL-DATA CATEGORY - caste, religion, health and sexual orientation are ordinary personal data. No Art.22-GDPR right against automated decision-making, no profiling provision

RBI Digital Lending Guidelines (Sept 2022) and Fair Practices Code contain NO geographic-discrimination prohibition; IRDAI underwriting regulations do not prohibit locality-based pricing (UNVERIFIED - counsel should confirm the negative)
Tenant screening is essentially unregulated; refusal to rent on grounds of religion or diet is documented and generally not actionable

Narrow criminal reach only: SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989 economic and social boycott provisions, and the Maharashtra Prohibition of People's Protection from Social Boycott Act 2016 (Maharashtra only)
CONSEQUENCE: the legal risk of enabling redlining in India is close to zero and the ethical risk is close to maximal. Because the law will not stop us, the architecture has to
evidence: Fetched en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redlining, which describes the US mechanism but contains nothing on crime maps in insurance, lending or tenant screening, and nothing on small-area disclosure mitigations. The Indian-law position above is from the agent's corpus and is asserted as a negative that counsel should confirm.
how_to_obtain: Ask counsel to confirm the negative: is there ANY Indian statutory or regulatory prohibition on geographic discrimination in lending, insurance underwriting or tenancy?
notes: Compounding factors: Indian residential segregation by caste and religion is empirically documented, so a fine-grained crime choropleth is substantially a map of where Muslims and Dalits live; and FIR density measures policing attention, not crime, so publishing it as 'crime' launders enforcement bias into apparent fact.

name: Statistical disclosure control and geographic anonymisation - the mitigation standard
publisher: UK ONS / US Census Bureau / police.uk (methodology, adopted here as design standard)
caveats: data.police.uk was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the police.uk anonymisation method below is UNVERIFIED and must be confirmed by the benchmark-product agent

Recollected police.uk method: incidents are snapped to a catalogue of pre-defined ANONYMOUS MAP POINTS, each chosen so the area it represents contains a minimum number of postal addresses; a point is NEVER placed on an actual address; only category and month are published
Primary suppression thresholds of n<5 or n<10 are conventional in SDC practice
Complementary suppression is required: suppressing one cell is useless if it can be back-calculated from row/column totals, so suppress a second cell or do not publish the total
A minimum population denominator per rendered unit is k-anonymity applied to geography: a 500-person ward with 3 thefts otherwise reads as a hotspot
None of this PREVENTS a determined actor from scraping polygons and building a screening product; it raises the cost and removes the precision that makes screening commercially attractive
evidence: WebFetch of data.police.uk/about returned EGRESS_BLOCKED. Wikipedia's Crime mapping article was fetched and explicitly contains nothing on geomasking, aggregation thresholds, suppression, property-value effects or police.uk. The method above is from the agent's corpus.
how_to_obtain: The benchmark-product agent should fetch data.police.uk/about and the Home Office 'anonymisation of street-level crime data' methodology note, and record the exact anonymous-map-point catalogue size, the minimum address count per point, and the licence.
notes: Proposed India rules: NO point geometry at all in v1 (polygons only); suppress any rendered cell with n<10; complementary suppression on category breakdowns and time series; rate-per-1000 as the only default with denominator visible; no unit with fewer than 5,000 residents rendered independently; coarse colour buckets with CIs on hover; no ranking endpoint; ToU prohibiting screening/underwriting/credit use.

name: IT Act 2000 s.79 - intermediary safe harbour, as read down in Shreya Singhal v Union of India
publisher: Parliament of India / Supreme Court of India
caveats: VERIFIED that Shreya Singhal declined to strike down ss.69A and 79 while striking down s.66A

UNVERIFIED detail: s.79(2) conditions (a) function limited to providing access to a communication system, (b) does not initiate the transmission, select the receiver or select/modify the information, (c) observes due diligence and prescribed guidelines; s.79(3)(a) conspiracy/abetment, s.79(3)(b) failure to expeditiously remove on actual knowledge

UNVERIFIED but important: Shreya Singhal v Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 READ DOWN s.79(3)(b) so that 'actual knowledge' means a COURT ORDER or a notification by the appropriate Government or its agency - NOT a private complaint. Strongly in our favour
THE CRITICAL LINE: s.79 protects THIRD-PARTY content only. Our computed heat map, category assignments and editorial framing are FIRST-PARTY publications with NO safe harbour
evidence: Fetched en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_Technology_Act,_2000. Confirms the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal struck down s.66A but 'turned down a plea to strike down sections 69A and 79 of the Act', and that the IT Rules 2021 supersede the 2011 Intermediary Guidelines. The article does not quote s.79 itself.
how_to_obtain: Read s.79 on indiacode.nic.in and the Shreya Singhal judgment on indiankanoon.org from an unblocked network.
notes: Design consequence: keep user-submitted reports on a separate layer, visually distinct, explicitly attributed to users, never merged into the statistical layer, and never used as an input to our own published aggregates.
